questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.description:

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

- At most 3 claims are checked per message, one argument per sentence.
- Results are verified, irrelevant, contradicted (unknown ID or wrong figure, which costs trust) or duplicate.
- Tolerance is ±0.5 pp on percentages, otherwise ±0.5%.
- Citing a rival quote reveals it to that supplier.

**Deadlines and limits** (`api.md:98-105,451-470`) [C]
- Each buyer message has 60 s per thread, counted from that thread's last supplier reply.
- Three consecutive timeouts end the thread.
- The default round limit is 10.
- Limits per key are 10 calls/s and 10 open sessions.
- The practice quota is 200 sessions per team per rolling 24 h (`api.md:52,84-85`; `starter-kit/README.md`; `AK/sim.py:32`).
- The claim that "arena.tacto.ai says no quota" is not in the repo. It is an external assumption [A] and is listed under the questions.

**Final** (`api.md:428-449`, `brief.md:161-204`, `submission.md:17-38`) [C]
- There are 5 waves with an 8-minute hard cap each. At the cap, open sessions score the alternative.
- There is one attempt per case and no human in the loop. The agent must not read `/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard` or `/results`.
- Code freezes Sunday 12:00, and no keys may be in the repo.

### Costly failure modes
1. A must-have breach through standard-term fill-ins scores 0, which is worse than walking.
2. Optimising price instead of C. Shorter terms, faster payment, a costlier incoterm and an index clause can all raise C.
3. Committing volume above need.
4. Accepting a sheet with `missing_fields`.
5. Accepting with C ≥ C_alt. `closing_move` uses `c_alt = inf` when the alternative is `none` (`AK/play.py:130`), so it accepts any must-have-passing sheet even above C_open, which scores 0 anyway.
6. Contradicted or duplicate citations, or more than 3 claims in a message. `guard` drops unknown IDs but does not cap claims, dedupe or check figures (`AK/agents/llm.py:168-183`) [C].
7. Leaking the alternative, the budget or urgency. `prepare()` puts the whole case JSON, including the buyer block, into the prompt (`llm.py:108`). `render()` adds "Your alternative... C = ..." (`llm.py:127`). Nothing checks the output for leaks [C].
8. Pushing after `final_offer`.
9. Late replies. The LLM timeout is 45 s per attempt (`llm.py:60,82`) against the 60 s limit (`play.py:26`).
   - Whether the SDK retries on top of that is [A]. Set `max_retries=0`.
   - Attachment downloads (`play.py:118-123,178`) and the fallback share the same 60 s window.
   - `play()` only logs a warning after 45 s (`play.py:160-161`). No deadline is enforced [C].
10. Open sessions at the wave cap.
11. The relationship term is never passed. `relationship_cost` returns 0 without a supplier estimate (`cost.py:111-122`). `closing_move` (`play.py:135`), `render` (`llm.py:132`) and `guard` (`llm.py:160`) call `total_cost` without one [C].
12. RFQ threads are served serially. `play()` handles one thread per loop iteration (`play.py:152-181`) and `table.send()` blocks for the supplier reply, which can take about a minute (`api.md:457`). While thread A is sent, thread B's 60 s clock keeps running [C].
13. Any non-409 `ArenaError` aborts the case. `play.py:168-170` re-raises 422, 429 and 5xx once the client retries are exhausted. The session then stays open until the cap and scores the alternative [C].
14. A late send is recorded as a sent offer. After a 409, `play.py:172-178` calls `missed()` and then appends the unsent message as a buyer message [C].
    - The arena repeats the buyer's last offer instead (`api.md:454`), so the thread history can hold phantom offers and `moves_left` can miscount.

## 2. Existing stack and what to reuse

- **Reuse as is** [C]:
  - `AK/play.py`: the loop, `closing_move`, `play_waves` and 409 resume.
  - `AK/client.py`: the sync client with a per-client pacer (`client.py:14,53-58`).
  - `AK/cost.py`: `total_cost`, `complete_offer`, `must_haves_ok`.
  - `AK/sim.py`: the local simulator.
  - `AK/docs.py`: `standard_terms`.
  - `AK/agents/llm.py`: `complete(system,user)->str` with a JSON reply, validated by `guard`.
- **Extend** [C]: the relationship wiring, a shared accept check, hardened fallback, an enforced deadline, claim verification, an allow-listed prompt and error handling in `play()`.

## 3. Proposed architecture

Keep the stack. Add a small deterministic layer around one LLM call per turn. Do not build a multi-agent framework and do not add a separate Closer role.

| Role | Type | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prepare (once per case) | Deterministic SQL, optionally one LLM summary | case, `DataPackage` | Dossier: evidence cards `{id, fact, figure}` (only IDs whose record holds a figure), justified-move calc, one supplier cost estimate for the relationship term |
| Strategy, terms and message (per turn) | One LLM call, 25-30 s timeout | Dossier, thread events, candidate packages (seeds), previous `notes` | JSON: `term_sheets` (validated by code), `claims` as `{id, figure}`, `body`, free-text `notes`, optional approval/role flag |
| Evaluate and validate | Deterministic | proposed sheets, standing sheets, case | C including the relationship term, must-haves, no-regression, claim cap, dedupe and figure tolerance, leak check |
| Accept or walk | Deterministic, one shared `accept_ok(case, threads, sid)` | standing sheets, alternative | used by `closing_move`, `guard` and `NaiveAgent` |

**State**
- State stays in `threads` (the events list). Used claims and pushed-after-final are derived by small pure helpers, not a second `Ledger` store.
- The only new memory is the LLM's `notes` string, fed back next turn.
- Offer history is built from the arena's thread data. Late sends are not recorded as offers.

**Handoffs**
- The ranker only seeds candidates in the prompt.
- The LLM proposes terms and code validates them with `complete_offer`, must-haves, no-regression and a price floor.
- Claims are rendered from the Dossier in code, so the figure always matches the fact row.
- The single fallback is `NaiveAgent` hardened with `accept_ok`. It is precomputed before the LLM call.

### One negotiation turn
1. `play()` gets the reply, fetches attachments and parses standard terms (`play.py:142-181`).
2. Re-read `seconds_left` and the per-thread deadline (about 35 s from the supplier reply).
3. If near the cap, run `closing_move` using `accept_ok`.
4. Precompute the fallback move and the ranked seed packages (C with the relationship estimate).
5. If `accept_ok` is satisfied and status is `final_offer`, or rounds are nearly out, send accept.
6. Call the LLM with the allow-listed case view, the Dossier, the seeds, the events and the previous `notes`. Expect JSON.
7. Validate:
   - sheets are complete and valid;
   - no must-have breach;
   - no regression against our previous sheet or the supplier's;
   - at most 3 claims, each ID in the Dossier and not repeated;
   - no leaked limits.
8. On failure or timeout, send the precomputed fallback.
9. Send. On 422, resend the deterministic sheet. On a late 409, record a timeout, not an offer. Loop.

**RFQ**: run one worker per thread (or send each round concurrently) so thread B's clock does not run out while A is served. Never accept before comparing all live sheets.

## 4. Negotiation behavior

- **Interest inference**:
  - Compute the justified cost move from drivers × idx changes.
  - Use the supplier performance gap (`sc`, `qn`), volume stability (`fc`) and cash sensitivity (`credit_index`, `equity_ratio`, `skonto_*`, late payments).
  - Use the settled-versus-asked pattern and correspondence themes.
  - Treat all of these as ranked hypotheses [A]. The LLM states them in `notes`.
- **Tone**: do not model emotions. Track observable signals (status, `final_offer`, timeouts, concession per round, reply delay). Keep the tone neutral, factual and short.
- **Stabilise and secure_supply**: use the relationship estimate as an advisory price floor until hosted practice validates it. Its source is a `should_cost` row or a `cost_drivers`-based estimate. Provide it through one `total_cost` wrapper used at every call site.
- **Packages**: send 2-3 sheets enumerated from `term_options` and ranked by C. Examples are price/payment pairs, longer contract at lower price, and incoterm swaps. Offer cheap-for-us items (volume visibility, 30-day payment) for a larger price move.
- **Roles and approvals**: no thresholds are documented (`brief.md:38-46`) [A]. The LLM flags a role or approval request in `notes` and re-engages with whoever replies. No deterministic rule until replays show a pattern.
- **Accept**:
  - The standing sheet must be the lowest C among live threads.
  - Must-haves must pass on the closing terms.
  - C must be below C_alt, with a margin.
  - There must be no missing fields, or the fill-ins must be priced.
  - Either status is `final_offer` or rounds are nearly out.
- **Walk**: walk when no sheet passes. Make `closing_move` choose the walking thread deliberately and not `live_threads()[0]` (`play.py:138`), which ends a whole RFQ.
- **Privacy**:
  - Build the prompt from an allow-listed case view, not `json.dumps(case)`.
  - Add output checks for numbers equal to C_alt, the budget or the rates.
  - Do not cite rival quotes unless the leak is intended.

## 6. Implementation plan and metrics

**Priority order**
1. **Baseline hardening (milestone 1)**: shared `accept_ok`, naive hardening, relationship estimate wiring, and synthetic unit tests for must-haves and alternatives.
2. **Error and deadline handling**: 422/5xx in `play()`, a 35 s decision deadline, 409 late-send fix, `max_retries=0`, and an RFQ per-thread worker with a delayed-reply test on S02.
3. **Guard and prompt**: allow-listed prompt, structured claims with code-rendered figures, claim cap, dedupe and leak check, and the `notes` memory.
4. **Dossier and package seeds**.
5. **Hosted practice**, budgeted against 200 sessions per 24 h:
   - Run the 10 playable cases and read each replay.
   - Compare c_deal with c_best, and classify losses (wrong package, early accept, contradicted claim, timeout).
   - Check suppliers across profiles (squeezed family firm, pruned small account, large stable supplier, RFQ pair).
6. **Supplier simulator** as a `Sim._answer` replacement, only once replays show how suppliers behave.
7. **Latency and concurrency**:
   - Run `--parallel` up to 10 with the real clock.
   - Size the pool to the wave's cases and log queue delay.
   - Measure close-call latency and set `CLOSE_BEFORE_CAP_S` from it.
   - Re-read `seconds_left` before each decision.
   - Budget about 3-4 rounds per thread per wave [A].
8. **Fallbacks and restart**: LLM down, parse failure, 409, 422, 429, 5xx. Each must end in a valid deterministic move or an explicit walk.
   - Add a start-up reconcile for the final runner: list sessions, resume open ones, never open blindly, and run a single runner per key.
   - Test the 409 resume path. It depends on the `RUNNING` regex wording (`play.py:30`).
9. **Final rehearsal** from the final machine and network, with all cases parallel, finishing well inside 8 minutes. Re-run `arena data` after the Sunday release. Check the commit hash and that the README lists env var names only (`submission.md:5-15,31-38`).

**Success metrics**
- Mean hosted-practice case score against the naive baseline. Local naive scores 0.52 / 0.51 / 0.68 [A, carried over from an explorer and not re-run]. They only check plumbing.
- Zero must-have breaches and zero accepts with C ≥ C_alt.
- Contradicted-claim rate near 0.
- Fraction of cases closed before the cap.
- p95 decision latency under 35 s from the supplier reply, with zero timeouts.
- Zero unhandled exceptions across 10 parallel sessions.
- Gap C_deal − C_best per supplier profile.

## First milestone
Shared `accept_ok`, hardened `NaiveAgent` and `closing_move` (including picking the best RFQ thread), relationship estimate wiring, and unit tests on synthetic must-have and alternative cases. The goal is an agent that cannot score 0 through a must-have breach or accept worse than the alternative. It needs no hosted quota and no new LLM design.

{
  "summary": "Read-only exploration of the Tacto Negotiation Arena kit, then a verified architecture and implementation report",
  "agentCount": 11,
  "logs": [
    "explorers returned: 6/6",
    "verification issues: 25"
  ],
  "result": "# Tacto Negotiation Arena: buyer exploration report (revised)

Tags: **[C]** = confirmed by reading the source or running local code; **[A]** = assumption. Paths are relative to `/Users/osama.salem/Documents/ehl`. `starter-kit/arena_kit` is abbreviated `AK` (`AK/agents/llm.py` = `starter-kit/arena_kit/agents/llm.py`). Local sim cases live at `AK/sim_cases/`. No hosted API calls were made and the `.env` files were not read. Only local code ran (`cost.total_cost`, `pytest`).

## 1. Challenge and data

### Confirmed rules

**Docs and data**
- The authoritative docs are `brief/brief.md`, `brief/api.md` and `brief/submission.md` (`starter-kit/README.md:7`) [C].
- The data package is the repo-root `data/` folder. It is read through `ARENA_DATA` (`starter-kit/README.md:38`, `AK/cli.py:62`) [C].
- The Sunday release and the hidden cases are not available locally [C].
- Citable IDs have the form `<type>:<id>[@period]` (`brief/brief.md:91`) [C].

**Cases and goals**
- Case types are price_increase, renewal, rfq, bundling, raw_material, capacity and quality (`brief/api.md:312`) [C].
- An RFQ has 2-3 supplier threads, and accepting one ends the case [C].
- Category goals are stabilise, secure_supply, quality_first, leverage and routine. The goal sets the rates (`api.md:332-335`, `AK/cost.py:15-16`) [C].
- Only stabilise and secure_supply add the supplier-health (relationship) cost term [C].
- Hosted practice has 19 case files, 10 of them playable. The final is hidden, in 5 waves (`brief/brief.md:59-60`) [C].

**What the local sim covers**
- The sim has only S01 (price_increase, leverage), S02 (rfq, leverage) and S03 (renewal, routine) (`AK/sim_cases/S01-S03.json`) [C].
- All three have empty `must_haves`, and none is a stabilise or secure_supply case [C].
- So the local sim cannot exercise the must-have path or the relationship term. Both need synthetic unit-test cases.

**Total cost C** (`api.md:377-417`, `AK/cost.py:55-167`) [C]
- C = spend + uncovered need at the fallback price × (1 + risk) + payment-term interest + freight + late cost + defect cost + tooling + index adjustment and risk + relationship.
- Payment interest is `spend*r*(d_ref-payment_days)/360`.
- A contract shorter than the horizon pushes the uncovered need to the fallback price.
- I recomputed S03 with `cost.total_cost` at 217.77, 60 days and FCA. 12 months costs 4,118,431 and 24 months costs 3,771,767, so 12 months is about 347k worse. This matches the brief's "same price for 12 months scores worse than opening" (`brief.md:154-160`).
- I recomputed S01 at 15.88. Cost is 107,730 at 60 days and 108,809 at 14 days (+1,079). Moving 60→30 or 60→90 days shifts cost by about 704 either way. Each +0.10 EUR of unit price adds about 665.

**Score** (`AK/cost.py:171-176`) [C]
- Case score = clip((C_open − C_deal)/(C_open − C_best), 0, 1).
- No deal scores the alternative, and 0 if the alternative is `none`.
- A wave is the mean of its case scores × 100, so the total is at most 500.

**Must-haves**
- A deal that breaks a must-have scores 0.
- The check runs on the closing terms, which include the supplier's standard terms for unsent fields (`cost.py:178-186`, `api.md:338`) [C].

**Alternative**
- It is `none`, a `quote` or the `current_contract`. If C_alt ≤ C_deal, walk or let the case time out (`api.md:339,423-426`) [C].
- Never reveal it, or the lack of one.

**Term sheets and acceptance** (`api.md:95-105,196,233-236`, `cost.py:27-44`) [C]
- Only term sheets bind. A buyer sheet carries exactly the negotiable fields, with values from `term_options`, and at most 3 sheets go in a message.
- Violations return 422 and cost no round.
- Only the buyer closes, by accepting the supplier's standing sheet id. Status `agreed` still needs an accept.
- Gaps close on the supplier's quote-PDF standard terms. An unknown incoterm is priced at the costliest freight.

**Claims** (`api.md:238-260`) [C]
- At most 3 claims are checked per message, one argument per sentence.
- Results are verified, irrelevant, contradicted (unknown ID or wrong figure, which costs trust) or duplicate.
- Tolerance is ±0.5 pp on percentages, otherwise ±0.5%.
- Citing a rival quote reveals it to that supplier.

**Deadlines and limits** (`api.md:98-105,451-470`) [C]
- Each buyer message has 60 s per thread, counted from that thread's last supplier reply.
- Three consecutive timeouts end the thread.
- The default round limit is 10.
- Limits per key are 10 calls/s and 10 open sessions.
- The practice quota is 200 sessions per team per rolling 24 h (`api.md:52,84-85`; `starter-kit/README.md`; `AK/sim.py:32`).
- The claim that "arena.tacto.ai says no quota" is not in the repo. It is an external assumption [A] and is listed under the questions.

**Final** (`api.md:428-449`, `brief.md:161-204`, `submission.md:17-38`) [C]
- There are 5 waves with an 8-minute hard cap each. At the cap, open sessions score the alternative.
- There is one attempt per case and no human in the loop. The agent must not read `/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard` or `/results`.
- Code freezes Sunday 12:00, and no keys may be in the repo.

### Costly failure modes
1. A must-have breach through standard-term fill-ins scores 0, which is worse than walking.
2. Optimising price instead of C. Shorter terms, faster payment, a costlier incoterm and an index clause can all raise C.
3. Committing volume above need.
4. Accepting a sheet with `missing_fields`.
5. Accepting with C ≥ C_alt. `closing_move` uses `c_alt = inf` when the alternative is `none` (`AK/play.py:130`), so it accepts any must-have-passing sheet even above C_open, which scores 0 anyway.
6. Contradicted or duplicate citations, or more than 3 claims in a message. `guard` drops unknown IDs but does not cap claims, dedupe or check figures (`AK/agents/llm.py:168-183`) [C].
7. Leaking the alternative, the budget or urgency. `prepare()` puts the whole case JSON, including the buyer block, into the prompt (`llm.py:108`). `render()` adds "Your alternative... C = ..." (`llm.py:127`). Nothing checks the output for leaks [C].
8. Pushing after `final_offer`.
9. Late replies. The LLM timeout is 45 s per attempt (`llm.py:60,82`) against the 60 s limit (`play.py:26`).
   - Whether the SDK retries on top of that is [A]. Set `max_retries=0`.
   - Attachment downloads (`play.py:118-123,178`) and the fallback share the same 60 s window.
   - `play()` only logs a warning after 45 s (`play.py:160-161`). No deadline is enforced [C].
10. Open sessions at the wave cap.
11. The relationship term is never passed. `relationship_cost` returns 0 without a supplier estimate (`cost.py:111-122`). `closing_move` (`play.py:135`), `render` (`llm.py:132`) and `guard` (`llm.py:160`) call `total_cost` without one [C].
12. RFQ threads are served serially. `play()` handles one thread per loop iteration (`play.py:152-181`) and `table.send()` blocks for the supplier reply, which can take about a minute (`api.md:457`). While thread A is sent, thread B's 60 s clock keeps running [C].
13. Any non-409 `ArenaError` aborts the case. `play.py:168-170` re-raises 422, 429 and 5xx once the client retries are exhausted. The session then stays open until the cap and scores the alternative [C].
14. A late send is recorded as a sent offer. After a 409, `play.py:172-178` calls `missed()` and then appends the unsent message as a buyer message [C].
    - The arena repeats the buyer's last offer instead (`api.md:454`), so the thread history can hold phantom offers and `moves_left` can miscount.

### Datasets
Counts were verified by read-only SQLite on `data/world.sqlite` [C].

**Tables and keys**
- There are 24 tables with no declared FOREIGN KEYs. Joins use prefixed text IDs (`data/README.md:23-58`).
- Row counts: suppliers 447, parts 60, po_lines 5,400, invoices 5,578, quality_notifications 1,033, scorecards 414, forecasts 720, quotes 108, index_values 2,258, cost_drivers 166, should_cost 28, news 39, documents 208, contracts 46 (+280 clauses).
- Prices are per `price_unit` (1, 100 or 1,000), and currency is EUR.
- `data/facts.json` holds 10,356 citable IDs. `sup:`, `part:`, `gr:` and `inv:` IDs are not in it.

**Access caveats** (`AK/data.py:59-108`) [C]
- `lookup()` returns the thin facts record, so a cited figure is not always verifiable from it. Use `query()` for full rows.
- Tables whose first column is not an ID (price_conditions, cost_drivers, negotiation_history and others) are unreachable by `lookup()`. Use SQL.
- `DataPackage.cases` is empty locally.

**Quirks** (`data/KNOWN_ISSUES.md`, `data/SCORECARD.md`) [C]
- OTD differs by 10-30 points depending on requested versus confirmed dates.
- 83 po_lines carry `stale_condition` prices.
- Should-cost has 5-15% error.

### Trace: S01 (price_increase, part:320050, sup:70270)
- **Setup** (`AK/sim_cases/S01.json:3-61`) [C]:
  - Negotiable fields are unit_price and payment_days (14/30/45/60/90).
  - Fixed terms are 6,650 units/yr, 12 months, FCA, 42-day lead time, no must-haves, alternative `none`.
  - The buyer block has current 15.88, fallback 18.26, 8% interest and a 60-day reference.
  - `trigger_doc` is null, so the supplier's ask is unknown.
- **Price history**: 16.35 (2023), 15.46 (2024), 15.88 (2025), 15.88 (2026) [C].
- **negotiation_history**: asked +5.8% and settled +2.7% in 2025, then asked +2.8% and settled 0.0% in 2026 [C].
- **Cost drivers and indices**:
  - Weights are steel PPI-C2431 0.31, electricity PPI-D351 0.03 and labour LCI-C 0.36.
  - Steel rose 115.0→129.1 (+12.26%), so a steel-justified rise is capped near +3.8%.
  - The weights are an internal estimate, and `cost_drivers` has no citable ID [C].
  - LCI-C being a German index while the supplier is Czech is a caveat [A].
- **Contract and performance** [C]:
  - Contract `ctr:4600070270`: prices are fixed per calendar year with 90-day change notice (#3.1). The quality target is 95% OTD with a EUR 150 fee per complaint (#6.1).
  - The contract says EXW and 45 days net, while the case fixes FCA with a 60-day reference. Which governs is an open question.
  - Scorecard `sc:70270@2026Q3`: OTD 84.6% (88.5% against confirmed dates), ppm 1,531, amber, improving.
- **Forecast and payments**:
  - `fc:320050@2026-09` is 6,650 units, matching the need [C].
  - Hollerau pays on average 5.4 days late, so "we always pay on time" would be contradicted [C].
- **Correspondence**:
  - The owner expects a partnership return for the 2022 old-price quarter (`doc:20260318-70270-M3`) [C].
  - The sales director is pruning small accounts (`doc:20260223-70270-M2`) [C].
  - The owner uses a two-year-old cost spreadsheet (`doc:20260809-70270-M1`) [C].
- **Evidence uses**:
  - The idx pair gives a justified-increase ceiling.
  - The `ctr` clause and `sc` row give notice and OTD-gap arguments.
  - The `fc` row supports a volume offer. Payment history supports a payment-days trade.
  - Which meeting notes are quotable is [A].
- **Stabilise example**: the `part:310010` / `sup:70110` family has letter P01 asking +9.5% from 2026-11-01 on 51 days' notice against a 90-day clause. The supplier has accepted below-cost prices before, so the relationship term bites there [C].

### Unknowns [A]
- Hosted suppliers are LLM-driven. Approval thresholds, tone effects and the contradicted-claim penalty are undocumented.

## 2. Existing stack and what to reuse

- **Reuse as is** [C]:
  - `AK/play.py`: the loop, `closing_move`, `play_waves` and 409 resume.
  - `AK/client.py`: the sync client with a per-client pacer (`client.py:14,53-58`).
  - `AK/cost.py`: `total_cost`, `complete_offer`, `must_haves_ok`.
  - `AK/sim.py`: the local simulator.
  - `AK/docs.py`: `standard_terms`.
  - `AK/agents/llm.py`: `complete(system,user)->str` with a JSON reply, validated by `guard`.
- **Extend** [C]: the relationship wiring, a shared accept check, hardened fallback, an enforced deadline, claim verification, an allow-listed prompt and error handling in `play()`.

## 3. Proposed architecture

Keep the stack. Add a small deterministic layer around one LLM call per turn. Do not build a multi-agent framework and do not add a separate Closer role.

| Role | Type | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prepare (once per case) | Deterministic SQL, optionally one LLM summary | case, `DataPackage` | Dossier: evidence cards `{id, fact, figure}` (only IDs whose record holds a figure), justified-move calc, one supplier cost estimate for the relationship term |
| Strategy, terms and message (per turn) | One LLM call, 25-30 s timeout | Dossier, thread events, candidate packages (seeds), previous `notes` | JSON: `term_sheets` (validated by code), `claims` as `{id, figure}`, `body`, free-text `notes`, optional approval/role flag |
| Evaluate and validate | Deterministic | proposed sheets, standing sheets, case | C including the relationship term, must-haves, no-regression, claim cap, dedupe and figure tolerance, leak check |
| Accept or walk | Deterministic, one shared `accept_ok(case, threads, sid)` | standing sheets, alternative | used by `closing_move`, `guard` and `NaiveAgent` |

**State**
- State stays in `threads` (the events list). Used claims and pushed-after-final are derived by small pure helpers, not a second `Ledger` store.
- The only new memory is the LLM's `notes` string, fed back next turn.
- Offer history is built from the arena's thread data. Late sends are not recorded as offers.

**Handoffs**
- The ranker only seeds candidates in the prompt.
- The LLM proposes terms and code validates them with `complete_offer`, must-haves, no-regression and a price floor.
- Claims are rendered from the Dossier in code, so the figure always matches the fact row.
- The single fallback is `NaiveAgent` hardened with `accept_ok`. It is precomputed before the LLM call.

### One negotiation turn
1. `play()` gets the reply, fetches attachments and parses standard terms (`play.py:142-181`).
2. Re-read `seconds_left` and the per-thread deadline (about 35 s from the supplier reply).
3. If near the cap, run `closing_move` using `accept_ok`.
4. Precompute the fallback move and the ranked seed packages (C with the relationship estimate).
5. If `accept_ok` is satisfied and status is `final_offer`, or rounds are nearly out, send accept.
6. Call the LLM with the allow-listed case view, the Dossier, the seeds, the events and the previous `notes`. Expect JSON.
7. Validate:
   - sheets are complete and valid;
   - no must-have breach;
   - no regression against our previous sheet or the supplier's;
   - at most 3 claims, each ID in the Dossier and not repeated;
   - no leaked limits.
8. On failure or timeout, send the precomputed fallback.
9. Send. On 422, resend the deterministic sheet. On a late 409, record a timeout, not an offer. Loop.

**RFQ**: run one worker per thread (or send each round concurrently) so thread B's clock does not run out while A is served. Never accept before comparing all live sheets.

## 4. Negotiation behavior

- **Interest inference**:
  - Compute the justified cost move from drivers × idx changes.
  - Use the supplier performance gap (`sc`, `qn`), volume stability (`fc`) and cash sensitivity (`credit_index`, `equity_ratio`, `skonto_*`, late payments).
  - Use the settled-versus-asked pattern and correspondence themes.
  - Treat all of these as ranked hypotheses [A]. The LLM states them in `notes`.
- **Tone**: do not model emotions. Track observable signals (status, `final_offer`, timeouts, concession per round, reply delay). Keep the tone neutral, factual and short.
- **Stabilise and secure_supply**: use the relationship estimate as an advisory price floor until hosted practice validates it. Its source is a `should_cost` row or a `cost_drivers`-based estimate. Provide it through one `total_cost` wrapper used at every call site.
- **Packages**: send 2-3 sheets enumerated from `term_options` and ranked by C. Examples are price/payment pairs, longer contract at lower price, and incoterm swaps. Offer cheap-for-us items (volume visibility, 30-day payment) for a larger price move.
- **Roles and approvals**: no thresholds are documented (`brief.md:38-46`) [A]. The LLM flags a role or approval request in `notes` and re-engages with whoever replies. No deterministic rule until replays show a pattern.
- **Accept**:
  - The standing sheet must be the lowest C among live threads.
  - Must-haves must pass on the closing terms.
  - C must be below C_alt, with a margin.
  - There must be no missing fields, or the fill-ins must be priced.
  - Either status is `final_offer` or rounds are nearly out.
- **Walk**: walk when no sheet passes. Make `closing_move` choose the walking thread deliberately and not `live_threads()[0]` (`play.py:138`), which ends a whole RFQ.
- **Privacy**:
  - Build the prompt from an allow-listed case view, not `json.dumps(case)`.
  - Add output checks for numbers equal to C_alt, the budget or the rates.
  - Do not cite rival quotes unless the leak is intended.

## 6. Implementation plan and metrics

**Priority order**
1. **Baseline hardening (milestone 1)**: shared `accept_ok`, naive hardening, relationship estimate wiring, and synthetic unit tests for must-haves and alternatives.
2. **Error and deadline handling**: 422/5xx in `play()`, a 35 s decision deadline, 409 late-send fix, `max_retries=0`, and an RFQ per-thread worker with a delayed-reply test on S02.
3. **Guard and prompt**: allow-listed prompt, structured claims with code-rendered figures, claim cap, dedupe and leak check, and the `notes` memory.
4. **Dossier and package seeds**.
5. **Hosted practice**, budgeted against 200 sessions per 24 h:
   - Run the 10 playable cases and read each replay.
   - Compare c_deal with c_best, and classify losses (wrong package, early accept, contradicted claim, timeout).
   - Check suppliers across profiles (squeezed family firm, pruned small account, large stable supplier, RFQ pair).
6. **Supplier simulator** as a `Sim._answer` replacement, only once replays show how suppliers behave.
7. **Latency and concurrency**:
   - Run `--parallel` up to 10 with the real clock.
   - Size the pool to the wave's cases and log queue delay.
   - Measure close-call latency and set `CLOSE_BEFORE_CAP_S` from it.
   - Re-read `seconds_left` before each decision.
   - Budget about 3-4 rounds per thread per wave [A].
8. **Fallbacks and restart**: LLM down, parse failure, 409, 422, 429, 5xx. Each must end in a valid deterministic move or an explicit walk.
   - Add a start-up reconcile for the final runner: list sessions, resume open ones, never open blindly, and run a single runner per key.
   - Test the 409 resume path. It depends on the `RUNNING` regex wording (`play.py:30`).
9. **Final rehearsal** from the final machine and network, with all cases parallel, finishing well inside 8 minutes. Re-run `arena data` after the Sunday release. Check the commit hash and that the README lists env var names only (`submission.md:5-15,31-38`).

**Success metrics**
- Mean hosted-practice case score against the naive baseline. Local naive scores 0.52 / 0.51 / 0.68 [A, carried over from an explorer and not re-run]. They only check plumbing.
- Zero must-have breaches and zero accepts with C ≥ C_alt.
- Contradicted-claim rate near 0.
- Fraction of cases closed before the cap.
- p95 decision latency under 35 s from the supplier reply, with zero timeouts.
- Zero unhandled exceptions across 10 parallel sessions.
- Gap C_deal − C_best per supplier profile.

content.text:
The exploration is finished: 11 agents ran, the draft got 25 review issues, and the revised report below applies them. It was a read-only exploration, so no hosted calls were made, no quota was used and no `.env` file was read.

## What the challenge is
- **Docs:** the authoritative rules are in `brief/brief.md`, `brief/api.md` and `brief/submission.md` at the repo root. The data package is the root `data/` folder, with 24 tables in `data/world.sqlite` and 10,356 citable IDs in `data/facts.json`.
- **Score:** each case scores `clip((C_open − C_deal) / (C_open − C_best), 0, 1)`. Here C is total cost in euros. A wave is the mean of its case scores × 100, so the maximum is 500 over five waves. A deal that breaks a must-have scores 0.
- **Total cost** includes spend, the uncovered need priced at the fallback price, payment interest, freight, defects, an index adjustment and a supplier-health term.
- **Price alone misleads:** on the local case S03, a 12-month contract at the same price costs about 347k more than a 24-month one. A lower unit price can therefore lose.
- **Term sheets:** only buyer term sheets bind. Only the buyer closes, by accepting the supplier's standing sheet.
- **Claims:** at most 3 claims per message are checked, and an unknown ID or a wrong figure costs trust.
- **Limits:** 60 seconds per reply per thread, 10 rounds by default, and 8 minutes hard cap per wave in the final. Practice is limited to 200 sessions per 24 hours.
- **Final:** one attempt per case, no human in the loop, and the agent must not read `/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard` or `/results`.
- **Local sim:** it has only S01, S02 and S03. All three have empty must-haves and none is a `stabilise` or `secure_supply` case, so unit tests with synthetic cases have to cover must-haves and the relationship term.

## Gaps in the starter kit, confirmed in source
1. **Leaks and weak checks:** the LLM prompt includes the whole case JSON, with your alternative and cost rates. Nothing checks the output for leaks. `guard` doesn't cap claims, dedupe them or verify figures. `walk_away` is accepted unconditionally.
2. **Relationship term:** it is never passed to `total_cost`, so it is always 0.
3. **Closing:** `closing_move` accepts anything that passes the must-haves when the alternative is `none`. It also walks via `live_threads()[0]`, which ends a whole RFQ.
4. **Deadlines:** the LLM timeout is 45 seconds against a 60-second limit. No deadline is enforced, only a warning is logged.
5. **RFQ threads:** they are served one at a time, so the other threads' clocks run out while one is being sent.
6. **Errors:** a 422 or 5xx that survives the client's retries aborts the case, which then scores the alternative.
7. **Late sends:** a late send that gets a 409 is recorded as if it were a sent offer.

## Recommended architecture
Keep the existing stack and add a thin deterministic layer around one LLM call per turn. There is no multi-agent framework and no separate Closer role.
- **Prepare (once per case):** SQL builds a dossier of evidence cards and a justified-move calculation, plus one supplier cost estimate for the relationship term.
- **Turn (LLM):** it proposes term sheets, claims and the message body, and writes `notes` that feed the next turn. Code validates every sheet with `complete_offer`, must-haves, no-regression and a price floor. Claim figures are rendered from the dossier in code.
- **Accept or walk (code):** one shared `accept_ok` is used by `closing_move`, `guard` and `NaiveAgent`.
- **Fallback:** a precomputed move from a hardened `NaiveAgent`, with a 35-second decision deadline and `max_retries=0`.

## First milestone
Build the shared `accept_ok`, harden `NaiveAgent` and `closing_move` (including choosing the best RFQ thread), wire in the relationship estimate, and add unit tests on synthetic must-have and alternative cases. The result is an agent that can't score 0 by breaking a must-have and can't accept a deal worse than the alternative. It needs no hosted quota and no new LLM design.

After that: 422/5xx and 409 handling, the allow-listed prompt and tighter `guard`, the dossier, then hosted practice, then final rehearsal.

## Open questions for the organizers
- Is the quota really 200 per 24 hours? A remote source reportedly says there is none.
- What does a contradicted claim cost, and are `EV-`, `sup:` and `part:` IDs and meeting notes citable?
- What is the no-deal score, and how is C_best computed on hosted cases?
- What are the approval thresholds for supplier roles?
- Which governs when a contract disagrees with the case? S01's contract says EXW and 45 days, while the case fixes FCA and 60 days.
- Is prompt injection against supplier bots allowed?

## Caveats on the report
- **Re-run and unchecked items:** the final reviewer didn't re-run pytest or the naive agent's local scores (0.52, 0.51 and 0.68). The SQLite row counts and the S01 trace were also not re-checked in the last pass.
- **Hosted suppliers:** they are LLM-driven and their behaviour isn't documented, so supplier-interest inference stays a hypothesis until practice runs show how they respond.

## Secrets still need cleaning up
The report found a local branch, `entire/d085602-e3b0c4`, whose commit 88ac6c5 modifies `.env.example`. It also found that `.gitignore` ignores only `.env`, not `.env.example`.
1. Move the keys into `starter-kit/.env` and restore the placeholders in `.env.example`.
2. Don't push any `entire/*` ref until you've checked it for keys.
3. Rotate the OpenAI key.

Submission rules forbid keys in the repo.

Should I start the first milestone and refresh CLAUDE.md alongside it? Starting it needs one decision from you: `LLM_MODEL` as `gpt-6-luna` or `gpt-6.1-sol`.

# Submission and pitch

What to hand in for the Tacto track, and how the pitch works. Deadline: **Sunday 12:00 on ehl.gg**.

## What to submit

1. **Your repo:** the agent and a README that says how to run it (setup, the environment variables it
   needs, without values, and the command). Put the **commit hash** your agent runs in the final into
   the description. The jury and tum.ai must be able to open the repo; tum.ai runs a code agent over
   every submission.
2. **A short description** of your approach: how your agent prepares, what it reads in the data, how
   it decides what to offer, and when it closes or walks away.
3. **Slides** for the pitch. The top 10 present them from 13:00.

Keep every key out of the repo: no `.env`, no LLM key, no arena key.

## At 12:00 your agent is already running

The code freeze and the Live Final start together, so start your agent before 12:00 and leave it
running:

```bash
uv run arena run --set final --agent llm --parallel 10
```

Or your own runner that polls `GET /v1/cases?set=final`. The kit's runner waits for wave 1, plays each
wave's cases in parallel within the 8-minute cap and stops after the fifth wave. From 12:00 there is no
human in the loop, and your agent must not read `/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard` or `/results`.
We check the top 10 for pushes after the freeze.

Checklist for 11:30:

- The machine and network you use for the final; one practice case went through it at the 09:00
  pre-flight.
- `uv run arena data` ran after 08:00, so the Sunday release sits next to the package.
- `uv run arena me` answers with your team: the key works.
- LLM credits and rate limits for about an hour of parallel play.
- The runner is started and logs to a file; the laptop is on power and does not sleep.

## The pitch

- **The top 10:** the ten teams with the most points after the five waves.
- **5 minutes pitch + 2 minutes of questions**, from 13:00. tum.ai keeps the time; the slot does not
  stretch.
- **Every replay is open to the jury.** After the final, each case on https://arena.tacto.ai/results
  links to its replay. Pick one negotiation and walk us through it.
- Questions to expect: Why did your agent write that? Would it have worked on a real supplier? What
  did your agent learn about suppliers, and from where?
- ⟦Q2: how the Live Final score and the jury combine for places 1-3, and the jury criteria⟧

1	**Procurement negotiation is a repeated business relationship under uncertainty.** Price matters, but so do supply continuity, quality, trust, internal approval, and whether both parties can deliver what they promise.
2	
3	For an agent, the challenge is to understand the commercial situation, make an appropriate move, and recognize when a person needs to take over.
4	
5	**1. What procurement actually involves**
6	
7	Procurement starts with a business need and continues through sourcing, contracting, delivery, performance management and eventual renewal or exit. Negotiation is one activity within that lifecycle. [CIPS procurement definition](https://1prd-dxp.cips.org/intelligence-hub/procurement/what-is-procurement).
8	
9	Consider a manufacturer buying a custom component:
10	
11	- Engineering needs the correct tolerances and material.
12	- Operations needs reliable delivery.
13	- Procurement wants competitive total cost.
14	- Finance cares about payment terms and working capital.
15	- Quality needs traceability and acceptable defect rates.
16	- The supplier needs margin, predictable demand and manageable production commitments.
17	
18	The negotiator must reconcile these interests. A cheaper component that causes production stoppages can be a worse purchase.
19	
20	**2. What the parties are negotiating**
21	
22	A deal is a package of interconnected terms.
23	
24	| Dimension | Buyer’s concern | Supplier’s concern |
25	|---|---|---|
26	| Price | Competitive cost | Adequate margin |
27	| Quantity | Avoid excess inventory | Economical production batches |
28	| Delivery | Availability and flexibility | Capacity and scheduling |
29	| Payment | Preserve cash | Receive cash predictably |
30	| Contract duration | Flexibility and continuity | Revenue certainty |
31	| Forecasts | Avoid overcommitment | Plan materials and capacity |
32	| Quality | Reliable performance | Feasible specifications |
33	| Risk allocation | Protection against failure | Avoid unmanageable obligations |
34	
35	This creates opportunities to trade across issues. A buyer might offer predictable volumes in exchange for a lower price, or faster payment in exchange for a discount.
36	
37	Presenting several packages of similar value to the buyer can also reveal what the supplier values most. This is the principle behind **multiple equivalent simultaneous offers**, or MESOs. [Harvard’s explanation](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/the-benefits-of-multiple-offers/).
38	
39	**3. The commercial concepts an agent needs**
40	
41	| Concept | Meaning | Example |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| Position | What a party explicitly asks for | “We need an 8% increase.” |
44	| Interest | The reason behind the position | Higher material costs or uncertain order volumes |
45	| Target | The preferred outcome | Keep the existing price |
46	| Reservation point | The least acceptable deal | Maximum acceptable total cost for a defined package |
47	| BATNA | Best alternative if agreement fails | Qualify another supplier or change the specification |
48	| ZOPA | The set of deals acceptable to both sides | Packages satisfying both parties’ limits |
49	| Authority | What the negotiator can commit to | May discuss pricing but cannot promise exclusivity |
50	
51	A BATNA must be realistic: an alternative supplier requiring six months of qualification may provide little leverage against a delivery needed next week. Harvard identifies alternatives as an important source of negotiating power. [Negotiation dynamics](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/tag/negotiation-dynamics/).
52	
53	**4. The lifecycle changes the negotiation**
54	
55	The following is a practical simplification of the broader [CIPS procurement cycle](https://1prd-dxp.cips.org/intelligence-hub/procurement/procurement-supply-cycle):
56	
57	| Stage | Main questions | Useful agent work |
58	|---|---|---|
59	| Define the need | What is essential? What can change? | Identify missing specifications and constraints |
60	| Understand the market | Who can supply? What are the alternatives? | Research suppliers and benchmark costs |
61	| Request offers | Are suppliers quoting comparable scopes? | Prepare RFQs and normalize quotations |
62	| Prepare negotiation | What are our priorities, limits and tradeable terms? | Build a mandate and evidence pack |
63	| Negotiate | What prevents agreement? Which package works? | Ask, propose, evaluate and track concessions |
64	| Approve and contract | Are the agreed terms complete and authorized? | Reconcile terms and route approvals |
65	| Deliver and manage | Did actual performance match the agreement? | Track delivery, quality and deviations |
66	| Renew or exit | Has the supplier earned more business? | Bring performance history into the next negotiation |
67	
68	Relationships accumulate history throughout this cycle. A supplier’s response today may reflect an unpaid invoice, an earlier broken forecast, or years of reliable collaboration.
69	
70	**5. Relationship and power**
71	
72	The appropriate approach depends on how much each party needs the other.
73	
74	For an easily replaceable standard item, competition and comparable quotations may dominate. For a specialized component with one qualified supplier, capacity, joint planning and continuity may matter more.
75	
76	A relationship has several dimensions:
77	
78	- **Dependability:** do both parties meet commitments?
79	- **Fairness:** are changes and concessions explained consistently?
80	- **Competence:** can the counterpart solve problems?
81	- **Transparency:** are relevant constraints disclosed?
82	- **History:** what happened in previous agreements?
83	
84	Close supplier relationships can support continuity and collaboration, especially with long-term suppliers. [CIPS supplier relationship guidance](https://cips-download.cips.org/fostering-collaboration-excelling-in-supplier-relationship-management).
85	
86	For an agent, relationship memory should record observable events: missed deliveries, resolved disputes, accepted concessions and fulfilled promises. A single “supplier sentiment score” loses much of that context.
87	
88	**6. Emotion and psychology**
89	
90	People negotiate on behalf of organizations, but experience the conversation personally. A supplier representative may worry about losing an account, appearing weak to a manager, or being blamed for an unprofitable agreement.
91	
92	Fisher and Shapiro identify five emotional concerns: **appreciation, affiliation, autonomy, status and role**. [Harvard’s discussion](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/teaching-negotiation-daily/managing-emotions-in-negotiation-teaching-students-to-turn-emotions-into-an-opportunity-for-mutual-gain/).
93	
94	Applied to procurement:
95	
96	| Concern | Practical implication |
97	|---|---|
98	| Appreciation | Acknowledge the supplier’s explanation before challenging it |
99	| Affiliation | Frame shared problems around delivery, quality or continuity |
100	| Autonomy | Offer meaningful options and allow room for internal review |
101	| Status | Avoid language that humiliates or dismisses the counterpart |
102	| Role | Recognize that the salesperson may need someone else’s approval |
103	
104	An agent should distinguish **observations from interpretations**:
105	
106	> Observation: “The supplier repeated ‘final offer’ and requested a call.”  
107	> Possible interpretations: limited authority, frustration, a firm boundary, or a negotiation tactic.
108	
109	It should not confidently label the person “angry” or “dishonest” from a short email. Clarification is often more useful than psychological speculation.
110	
111	Another relevant effect is **anchoring**: the first number can influence subsequent offers. The agent therefore needs an independent valuation before reacting to the supplier’s opening price. [Harvard on counteroffers](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/how-to-counteroffer-in-business-negotiation/).
112	
113	**7. What a negotiation turn should accomplish**
114	
115	A turn is a meaningful move: a question, explanation, proposal, concession, rejection, acceptance or escalation. It may contain several messages and involve several people.
116	
117	A useful agent turn follows this sequence:
118	
119	1. **Interpret:** what changed in the latest response?
120	2. **Update:** which terms, constraints or assumptions changed?
121	3. **Evaluate:** does the current package meet our objectives and limits?
122	4. **Choose:** ask, counteroffer, offer alternatives, pause, escalate or close.
123	5. **Validate:** is the proposed move accurate and authorized?
124	6. **Communicate:** make one clear move with an understandable rationale.
125	7. **Record:** preserve the offer version, commitments and unresolved points.
126	
127	There is no universal ideal number of turns. A clarification can produce more value than another price concession. Repeated counteroffers with no new information may indicate that the parties need a different package or a human conversation.
128	
129	**8. An illustrative negotiation**
130	
131	Suppose a supplier requests an increase from €10 to €10.80 per component.
132	
133	| Turn | Move | Purpose |
134	|---|---|---|
135	| 1 | Buyer asks for cost drivers and effective date | Understand the request |
136	| 2 | Supplier cites material costs and unpredictable small orders | Surface underlying interests |
137	| 3 | Buyer questions the full increase and asks about larger batches | Test a possible trade |
138	| 4 | Supplier offers €10.30 with scheduled releases | Put a conditional package forward |
139	| 5 | Buyer checks inventory implications with operations | Validate the internal tradeoff |
140	| 6 | Buyer proposes €10.20, scheduled releases and a review mechanism | Exchange value across terms |
141	| 7 | Supplier requests approval internally | Resolve authority |
142	| 8 | Both parties confirm the complete package | Prevent ambiguous agreement |
143	
144	These numbers are illustrative. The lesson is that order predictability can change the economics of the deal.
145	
146	**9. What this means for an agent system**
147	
148	The system should maintain more than a chat transcript:
149	
150	| Context | What to retain |
151	|---|---|
152	| Commercial mandate | Objectives, limits, priorities and approval authority |
153	| Evidence | Quotes, benchmarks, specifications and source dates |
154	| Deal state | Current packages, conditions and unresolved terms |
155	| Counterpart context | Stated interests, known constraints and uncertain hypotheses |
156	| Relationship history | Performance, disputes, concessions and commitments |
157	| Workflow state | Awaiting supplier, internal review, approval or signature |
158	
159	Success should be measured through **total value, supply reliability, policy compliance, relationship outcomes and realized performance**. A signed agreement is only an intermediate result; the procurement outcome becomes clear when the promised goods or services are delivered.

There is no universal ideal number of turns. A clarification can produce more value than another price concession. Repeated counteroffers with no new information may indicate that the parties need a different package or a human conversation.

**8. An illustrative negotiation**

Suppose a supplier requests an increase from €10 to €10.80 per component.

| Turn | Move | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buyer asks for cost drivers and effective date | Understand the request |
| 2 | Supplier cites material costs and unpredictable small orders | Surface underlying interests |
| 3 | Buyer questions the full increase and asks about larger batches | Test a possible trade |
| 4 | Supplier offers €10.30 with scheduled releases | Put a conditional package forward |
| 5 | Buyer checks inventory implications with operations | Validate the internal tradeoff |
| 6 | Buyer proposes €10.20, scheduled releases and a review mechanism | Exchange value across terms |
| 7 | Supplier requests approval internally | Resolve authority |
| 8 | Both parties confirm the complete package | Prevent ambiguous agreement |

These numbers are illustrative. The lesson is that order predictability can change the economics of the deal.

**9. What this means for an agent system**

The system should maintain more than a chat transcript:

| Context | What to retain |
|---|---|
| Commercial mandate | Objectives, limits, priorities and approval authority |
| Evidence | Quotes, benchmarks, specifications and source dates |
| Deal state | Current packages, conditions and unresolved terms |
| Counterpart context | Stated interests, known constraints and uncertain hypotheses |
| Relationship history | Performance, disputes, concessions and commitments |
| Workflow state | Awaiting supplier, internal review, approval or signature |

Success should be measured through **total value, supply reliability, policy compliance, relationship outcomes and realized performance**. A signed agreement is only an intermediate result; the procurement outcome becomes clear when the promised goods or services are delivered.

86	invoices and payments; quality notifications and quarterly scorecards (on-time delivery, PPM);
87	framework contracts and clauses; past RFQs and quotes; forecasts; supplier intel and news; past

99	
100	- **Round 0:** every supplier sends its quote e-mail at once, with a quote PDF.
101	- **Your message:** subject, body, up to 3 term sheets (each with a value for every negotiable
102	  field), the data IDs you rely on (IDs written in the body count too), optional text attachments.
103	- **The supplier answers by e-mail:** the role in charge writes; its standing term sheet; a status -
104	  `open`, `final_offer` (push further and it may walk), `agreed` (it offers exactly your terms; you
105	  still accept), `walked_away`, `no_bid`; signals (reply delay, quote validity); fields it left out;

109	  suppliers run in parallel threads; accepting one ends the case.
110	- **Limits:** a round limit per thread (default 10 messages) and **60 seconds per message**, counted
111	  from the supplier's reply. A late message counts as
112	  a timeout: your last offer repeated, the supplier's patience drops; three in a row, or one after
113	  the last round, end the thread.

117	you accept), a cost breakdown XLSX (ask; an open supplier sends one), an 8D report (quality), a

129	**category goal** - `stabilise`, `secure_supply`, `quality_first`, `leverage` or `routine` - and its
130	rates follow it. Reaching the goal is the skill.
131	
132	| Part of C | How |
133	|---|---|
134	| Price | committed units × unit price; units bought before a new price takes effect at the current price |
135	| Uncovered need | need the deal does not cover at the fallback price, plus the goal's fallback risk on it |
136	| Payment, freight, lead time | interest for paying earlier than your reference; freight by Incoterm; € per day beyond your need |

192	
193	**The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's

199	so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.
200	
201	The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
202	settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
203	- no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
204	the Sunday release.

207	
208	- **Top 10:** the 10 teams with the most points after the five waves pitch to our jury from 13:00:
209	  5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Every replay is open to the jury.
210	- **Track places 1-3** (open to all teams of the track): ⟦PLACEHOLDER - decided Sat morning:
211	  weighting of Live Final score vs. jury score, and the jury criteria (draft: approach,
212	  explainability, craft)⟧.
213	- **EHL Grand Final:** the best 2 of the 5 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final
214	  pitches. Finalist teams outside the top 10 are ranked by the Live Final score alone.
215	- **Ties:** points are points; an exact tie goes to more deals, then fewer rounds. At the top-10
216	  cut the jury looks at the score distribution. **Prizes:** €1,500 for 1st place, medals for the
217	  top 3, handed over by Tacto at the awards at 16:30.

220	
221	- **Numbers come from code, the model writes.** Compute C for every term sheet; put figures from
222	  the data next to their IDs; let the LLM choose arguments and wording.

227	- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget or a missing alternative. Don't take the first offer.
228	- **Plan your practice runs** (200 a day is for learning, not brute force) and **rehearse the
229	  final**: all hosted cases in parallel, from Sunday's machine and network, well inside 8 minutes.

opening quote. **C_best** is the cheaper of the best package any supplier in the case would ever
accept, with every valid lever applied, and your alternative - fixed per case, so good arguments
raise your score instead of moving the yardstick. **No deal** scores your alternative (0 if none);
some cases are best left without a deal. **A broken must-have** scores 0. **In the final** each
wave scores 0-100 (the mean of its case scores × 100, one decimal) and your **points so far** are the
sum of your wave scores - up to 500 after five waves. The formula is in `api.md`; `arena_kit.total_cost` computes C.

**Example** (a `leverage` case: 3 % fallback risk) - need 4,000 a year for 2 years, interest 8%,
reference 60 days. The foundry asks €43.20 for a 24-month contract at 30 days net.

| | Terms | C |
|---|---|---|
| C_open | €43.20, 30 days: 8,000 × 43.20 = 345,600, plus 30 days of early payment at 8% = 2,304 | €347,904 |
| Your deal | €41.60, 60 days: 8,000 × 41.60 = 332,800 | €332,800 |
| C_best (hidden) | €40.80, 90 days: 326,400, minus 30 days of interest saved = 2,176 | €324,224 |
| **Score** | (347,904 − 332,800) / (347,904 − 324,224) | **0.64** |

The same €41.60 for 12 months covers half your need; the rest counts at the fallback price, say
€46.00, plus 3 %: C = €355,920 - worse than the opening, score 0.

## 7. Rules

1. **Not allowed:** humans in the loop during the Live Final, attacks on the service or on other
   teams, more than one API key per team - and agents that read the live feed during the Live
   Final: the event feed, the screen and the leaderboard (`/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard`
   and their JSON).
2. **Everything else counts** - including weaknesses you find in our bots. Replays show how every
   score came about, and the jury may weigh that in the pitches. The goal is to convince a
   realistic supplier: that is what carries over to real negotiations.
3. **One attempt per case** in the final. An abandoned case is no deal.
4. **Code freeze at Sun 12:00.** Submit on ehl.gg: your repo (the agent and a README to run it), the
   commit hash, a short description and your pitch slides (`submission.md`). The final runs that
   commit, so your agent must be running and polling before 12:00. We check the top 10 for later
   pushes. Run your agent where you like, with your own LLM keys.
5. A supplier remembers only within a case; its history with your company is in the data.

## 8. The weekend

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Sat 10:00 | Kickoff and reveal: brief, data, kit, practice arena live |
| Sat 12:00-13:00 | Deep dive (ground floor, room on the signs): data, API, kit, Q&A - challenge selection closes 13:00 |
| Sat afternoon | Office hours at the Tacto table; practice all weekend |
| Sat ⟦TIME⟧ | Tacto stops answering for the night (Discord: https://discord.gg/hPwFfbWRV) |
| Sun 08:00 | **Sunday release:** new market news and letters (`/v1/data`) |
| Sun 09:00 | **Pre-flight:** one practice case through your final setup |
| Sun 12:00-~12:58 | **Code + slides freeze**, then the **Live Final** in 5 waves |
| Sun 13:00-14:30 | Top 10 pitch to the Tacto jury (5 min pitch + 2 min questions) |
| Sun 14:30 | Track winners and the two finalists announced |
| Sun 15:30 | Grand Final pitches (AudiMax) |
| Sun 16:30 | Awards |

**The Live Final.** The hidden cases come in **5 themed waves**. The host shows each wave's
theme on the big screen, then starts the wave; its cases appear at the start, for all teams at once,
each in its own order, one session per case. **Each wave has a hard cap of 8 minutes:** threads
still open at the cap end with no deal (your alternative's score). Start your agent before the
first wave and keep it running: it plays all of a wave's cases **in parallel** (up to 10 open
sessions per key) - the kit's `arena run --set final` does that. The leaderboard shows your points
so far, wave by wave; replays and the suppliers' back office appear after the final. A case broken on our side is replayed.

The hidden cases share the world, case types and rules of the practice set, with new suppliers and
settings. **Up to a third of them combine supplier types and case types that practice never shows**
- no new rules, but an agent that memorised the practice suppliers will meet strangers. Some cite
the Sunday release.

## 9. Selection and prizes

- **Top 10:** the 10 teams with the most points after the five waves pitch to our jury from 13:00:
  5 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Every replay is open to the jury.
- **Track places 1-3** (open to all teams of the track): ⟦PLACEHOLDER - decided Sat morning:
  weighting of Live Final score vs. jury score, and the jury criteria (draft: approach,
  explainability, craft)⟧.
- **EHL Grand Final:** the best 2 of the 5 EHL finalist teams in this track go on to the Grand Final
  pitches. Finalist teams outside the top 10 are ranked by the Live Final score alone.
- **Ties:** points are points; an exact tie goes to more deals, then fewer rounds. At the top-10
  cut the jury looks at the score distribution. **Prizes:** €1,500 for 1st place, medals for the
  top 3, handed over by Tacto at the awards at 16:30.

## 10. Tips

- **Numbers come from code, the model writes.** Compute C for every term sheet; put figures from
  the data next to their IDs; let the LLM choose arguments and wording.
- **Read the supplier** before you argue: its notes, letters, news and quote remarks tell you what
  it is dealing with - and what will move it.
- **Read the quote PDF** before you accept: what you did not negotiate closes on its standard terms.
- **Ask, and offer alternatives.** Two or three term sheets show you what a supplier values.
- **Don't leak** urgency, a budget or a missing alternative. Don't take the first offer.
- **Plan your practice runs** (200 a day is for learning, not brute force) and **rehearse the
  final**: all hosted cases in parallel, from Sunday's machine and network, well inside 8 minutes.
